newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian business welcomes foreign investment moves.
newsitem.headline: Indian business welcomes foreign investment moves.

text.p: Indian industrialists on Wednesday welcomed the government's decision to ease a restriction on foreign investment and its promise to step up economic reforms, saying they could spur growth.
The cabinet announced on Tuesday that foreign firms could take stakes of up to 74 percent in nine industrial sectors including infrastructure, non-conventional energy and electrical software.

The government also decided to grant automatic approval to foreign companies seeking stakes of up to 51 percent in 16 other sectors. The moves were seen as part of an effort by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front coalition government to attract greater amounts of foreign investment into sectors which are starved of capital and crucial to economic growth.

"This is the first bold step on part of the United Front government towards achieving the target of foreign direct investment of $10 billion per annum as envisaged in the common minimum programme," the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) said in a statement.
It was referring to a goal spelled out in June by the United Front in a policy blueprint.

"These changes would make foreign investment norms more transparent and attract foreign investors in infrastructure sectors," N. Mohanty, the highest ranking civil servant in the Industry Ministry, told Reuters.
The Industry Ministry said 1,401 foreign direct investment (FDI) proposals worth 343.6 billion rupees ($9.6 billion) were approved between January and November.
That was up from 1,335 proposals approved during the same period in 1995, worth 320.71 billion rupees ($8.9 billion).
The ministry said actual FDI inflows totalled 63.7 billion rupees ($1.78 billion) in 1995. Between January and October this year, actual inflows were 63.1 billion rupees ($1.76 billion).

Analysts say actual foreign investment, crucial to paying for the expensive overhaul of infrastructure such as roads, ports and telecommunications, must pick up to ensure high levels of economic growth.
"The government now must put a policy framework in place to attract foreign investment in infrastructure," said Subra Subramanian, an analyst at securities firm H.G. Securities.
Deve Gowda met industry leaders for five hours on Tuesday and pledged to step up economic reforms to achieve a long-term goal of seven percent annual growth of gross domestic product.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said that by mid-January the government would announce a series of policy measures to stimulate industrial growth and a lacklustre capital market.
Chidambaram's pledge pepped up stock markets. The Bombay Stock Exchange's key index jumped 5.7 percent on Wednesday.
Industry leaders said the government's steps would boost investors' confidence and boost industrial growth.

"The announcements are a step in the right direction and we hope when implemented they arrest the current slide in industrial growth," V. Raghuraman, secretary general of Associated Chambers of Commerce (Assocham), told Reuters.

Deve Gowda told industrialists on Tuesday that industrial output was forecast to grow eight percent in the fiscal year ending on March 31, well below both the official target of 12 percent and the 12.1 percent rate in the previous fiscal year.
